title: Rather retreat a foot
hookLine: better to be the guest than the host, to retreat a foot than advance an inch (Tao Te Ching 69)
carry: never make light of the other side

lines: BACKING OFF HAS A BAD NAME.
A WARRIOR CHOOSES A FOOT BACK.
cards: Backing off has a bad name. Back down. Give ground.
Retreat. Lose face. In a heated argument, the person who steps back first can look like the one who lost.
Chapter sixty-nine of the Tao Te Ching quotes an old master of war, a man whose whole trade is fighting, and he chooses exactly that. He'd rather give up a foot than take an inch.

teach.b: First, the guest, not the host. The chapter quotes a strategist who doesn't dare to be the host; he'd rather be the guest. In Legge's reading, the host is the one who starts the war, and the guest is the one who answers.
Then the line that names today, in Legge's translation: "I do not dare to advance an inch; I prefer to retreat a foot."
Second, marching without marching. The chapter piles up strange pictures: advancing without seeming to move, baring an arm that isn't there, holding no weapon, facing no enemy.
It's someone who refuses to give a fight anything to push against. Third, the worst mistake.

teach.h: NEVER MAKE LIGHT OF THE OTHER.
teach.b: No calamity is greater, the chapter says, than making light of the opponent; do that, and I come close to losing my treasures.

Some readers hear the three treasures from two days ago: gentleness, economy, and not daring to be first. Legge reads it as gentleness. Underestimating the other side, in this picture, is how you lose your own gentleness.

When armies meet, the side that grieves will win. Not the angriest, not the most confident: the one that is sorry there's a fight at all. Most days the war is smaller: a group chat, a dinner table, a parking spot.
A foot back might mean letting the other person speak first, taking their point seriously, and caring that the two of you are at odds. That isn't losing. It's refusing to make light of anyone.

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching, including students of strategy and the martial arts, take chapter sixty-nine as a teaching on restraint: answer rather than start, never underestimate the other side, and fight, if at all, with sorrow.

o: giving ground rather than pushing forward in a fight
the length of one stride in an ancient army's march
a rule that soldiers must stand a foot apart in line

p: would rather be guest than host

s: chapter sixty-nine says the confident side wins
it says that when armies meet, the side that grieves will win.
the chapter warns that making light of the opponent risks losing one's treasures
there's no calamity greater, it says, than underestimating the opponent.

games.q: two armies face each other. chapter sixty-nine names the one that wins. which?
games.why: the chapter says the side that grieves will win: not the angriest, but the one sorry there's a fight at all.

practice: Bring to mind one disagreement that's live right now, and see the other person clearly, not as a cartoon. In your mind, take one foot back: let them speak first, and hear their point at full strength, not the weakest version of it.
Then notice whether there's some sorrow underneath, that you're on opposite sides at all, and let it be there.

wordCard.voice: A foot back. In chapter sixty-nine, the old strategist would rather retreat a foot than advance an inch. Today's word.
